IN THE ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD
APPELLANT BY: Raja Ghanim Aabir Khan and Mr.
STATE BY: Mr. Osama Azeem Chaudhry, State
body: BABAR SATTAR, J.- Through this judgment we will decide (i) Criminal Appeal No. 171/2019 filed by Attaullah against the judgment of the learned Sessions Judge dated 18.05.2019, whereby he has been found guilty under section 302(b) of PPC and sentenced to death and has been held liable to pay compensation to the legal heirs of Junaid Mustafa deceased in the amount of Rs.500,000/- in terms of section 544-A, Cr.P.C, and in default of payment or recovery of compensation undergo further imprisonment for a period of six months (S.I) and has been convicted under section 392 of PPC and sentenced to ten years rigorous imprisonment with fine in the amount of Rs.100,000/-, and (ii) Murder Reference No. 13/2019, whereby the judgment of the learned Sessions Judge, East-Islamabad dated 18.05.2019, through which he has found Attaullah guilty for an offence under section 302(b) of Pakistan Penal Code, 1860 (“PPC”) and Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 2 sentenced him to death, has been referred to us under section 374 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, for confirmation.

2. Junaid Mustafa was a 26-year-old Careem Captain, who was murdered at 03.00 a.m on 22.02.2018 having been shot thrice at the edge of service road G-13/1 and Street 79, G-13/1, Islamabad. He stumbled into Street 79 and collapsed after walking a few meters. Noman Wahab (PW-8), who was a private night watchman hired by the residents of street 79, heard three gun shots, witnessed the collapse of the deceased Junaid Mustafa and heard him recite the Kalma before passing away. He informed the occupant of a nearby house. After a while rescue 1122 arrived and so did police officials and the body of the deceased was taken to Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) where postmortem of the body of the deceased was performed. According to the postmortem report the deceased had been shot thrice. One of the bullets entered and exited his wrist and two bullets hit his neck, inflicted considerable damage on his internal organs and caused his death.

3. The prosecution’s case is that the appellant, Attaullah, murdered Junaid Mustafa. Attaullah booked a ride through Careem App for pick-up in F-11 Markaz and was dropped off on the service road adjacent to Street 79, G-13/1, Islamabad. With the intent of robbing Junaid Mustafa of his vehicle (i.e. Suzuki Wagon R Stingray bearing No. AEG-658), Attaullah pointed a gun at Junaid Mustafa, who resisted and was consequently shot. During what transpired Attaullah dropped his CNIC at the edge of the service road which was recovered by the Investigating Officer, Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 3 Inspector Muhammad Riaz Gondal (PW-13). On the basis of the initial record provided by Careem, the Investigating Officer procured a profile photo of the customer who ordered the Careem Cab driven by Junaid Mustafa, which was that of Attaullah even though the customer’s name mentioned in the Careem’s database was Ifran Ullah. Attaullah meanwhile drove the vehicle after the incident to Mardan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. He then drove back the vehicle back to Islamabad on 22.02.20218 and parked it close to a roadside hotel (Chappar Hotel) in G-16/4 Islamabad, which was owned and managed by Attaullah’s father and three other people. Attaullah left the 30-bore pistol that he used to shoot the deceased Junaid Mustafa under the driver’s seat along with two magazines and ten bullets. On the basis of information supplied by an informer Attaullah was arrested from Islamabad Chowk at 11.00 a.m on 24.02.2018 while driving another stolen vehicle. He was interrogated. On his pointation the police recovered the vehicle on 27.02.2018 after Attaullah led the police party first to the roadside hotel and then pulled out the keys of the vehicle from a drawer in the hotel and led the police to the vehicle. From the vehicle the police recovered a 30-bore pistol, two magazines and ten bullets.

4. The case is one of circumstantial evidence where there is no eye-witness or direct evidence of the murder of Junaid Mustafa or the armed robbery attributed to the appellant, Attaullah. The learned Sessions Court has provided a summary of the evidence adduced by thirteen prosecution witnesses, which will be discussed subsequently in this judgment. The learned Sessions Court also examined three journalists as court witnesses but did Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 4 not rely on their testimony while finding Attaullah guilty of murder and armed robbery.

5. The prosecution’s case that convinced the learned Sessions Court that Attaullah had murdered Junaid Mustafa is built on three planks. The first is evidence of Attaullah booking a Careem Cab on 22.02.2022 in response to which the deceased Junaid Mustafa picked up Attaullah from F-11 Markaz Islamabad at 02.35 am and dropped him off at the corner of service road, and Street No.79, G-13/1 Islamabad at 02.58 am. The second plank of the prosecution’s case is that Attaullah in the process of shooting the deceased and robbing him off his vehicle dropped his CNIC at the place of occurrence (i.e. the corner of service road and street 79, G-13/1), which led to his identification by virtue of his profile photo for the account registered through mobile No. 0335-5167487 through which the Cab had been booked. While the mobile number was registered in the name of Irfan Ullah, the account was registered in the Careem system in the name of Attaullah and had his profile photo in the Careem database. The Investigating Officer thus matched the photo procured from the Careem system with the photo on the CNIC dropped by Attaullah at the place of occurrence and determined that Attaullah was the last person in touch with the deceased Junaid Mustafa, who robbed him of his vehicle and shot him in the process. The third plank of the prosecution’s case is two sets of recoveries. The first is the recovery of the cell phone which had the SIM No. 0335- 5167487 installed in it and the phone had the Careem App installed in it through which the Careem Cab had been ordered early morning on 22.02.2018. The second recovery was the Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 5 vehicle that was parked next to roadside hotel in G-16/4 supposedly co-owned and co-managed by appellant’s father. And it was Attaullah on whose pointation the recovery was made. And while the recovery was being made from a public place, Attaullah had exclusive knowledge of the vehicle’s key that he had hid inside the roadside hotel. Attaullah opened the vehicle using the key and the police then recovered the murder weapon (i.e. 30bore pistol) as well as magazines and bullets from under the driver’s seat.

6. The prosecution’s case is therefore built on the basis that evidence procured from Careem together with the recovery of the cell phone from Attaullah establishes that he ordered the Careem Cab driven by the deceased Junaid Mustafa on the fateful morning of 22.02.2018. This evidence while being in virtual mode acquires the form of last seen evidence establishing that the deceased Junaid Mustafa was last determined to be alive while driving the Careem Cab to pick up and drop Attaullah. The CNIC recovered from the place of occurrence then places Attaullah at such place at the time when Junaid Mustafa was shot. The night watchman, Noman Wahab (PW-8), witnessed him breathing his last on Street 79, G-13/1 at 3.00 am on 22.02.2018. And the vehicle that Junaid Mustafa was robbed of was subsequently recovered on the pointation of Attaullah who had exclusive knowledge of the hiding place of the key for such vehicle.

7. The motive was not pleaded in an explicit manner but is built within the prosecution story. Attaullah needed money as he was to marry soon. And to generate the required funds he began Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 6 stealing cars and disposing them off in alliance with his friend, Zubair Khan, who was based in Mardan, KP. He intended to steal the vehicle being driven by Junaid Mustafa as part of his vehicle– stealing-enterprise. And when the deceased resisted, Attaullah shot the deceased and fled with the vehicle. And he was subsequently arrested while driving another stolen vehicle.

8. The learned Sessions Court, however, did not dwell on the motive and whether it had been proved, and also made no observations with regard to Attaullah’s conviction under section 392 of PPC. While the learned Sessions Court did not state in its judgment that the motive stood proved, conviction of Attaullah for armed robbery under section 392 of PPC suggests that the learned Sessions Court deemed that the murder was driven by the intent to rob Junaid Mustafa of his vehicle.

9. Learned counsel for the appellant made the following submissions. There was no direct evidence against Attaullah and all the evidence adduced was circumstantial. SIM No. 0335- 5167487 was not registered in the name of Attaullah but Irfan Ullah, who had purportedly furnished an affidavit to the Investigating Officer stating that the SIM had been handed over to Attaullah. But Irfan Ullah never appeared as a witness to testify before the Court or produce any evidence. The phone purportedly recovered from the possession of Attaullah, which had SIM linked to the number 0335-5167487 installed in it, was not subjected to forensic examination to establish that it was in the use of Attaullah. The purported Careem App installed in the phone was also not subjected to forensic examination to establish that the Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 7 said App had been used to book Junaid Mustafa’s cab. The Security Manager of Careem, Qaiser Qayyum (PW-3), exhibited photo copies of documents printed out by Careem to establish the route of Junaid Mustafa’s cab, but no examination of Careem’s database had been undertaken to determine whether Junaid Mustafa’s Careem Cab had in fact been booked from the cell phone linked with SIM No. 0335-5167487. The empties were recovered from the place of occurrence on 22.02.2018 but were not sent for forensic examination till after the appellant was arrested on 24.02.2018 and the alleged murder weapon was recovered from the vehicle on 27.02.2018. Consequently any report stating that the empties sent for forensic examination on 27.02.2018 matched with the gun also recovered on 27.02.2018 and sent for forensic examination on 05.03.3018 was inconsequential. Likewise, the recovery of the vehicle from a public place was also inconsequential and there was no direct or corroborating evidence to establish that Attaullah had parked the vehicle from where it was recovered. There was also no independent evidence that Attaullah’s father was running the roadside hotel close to which the vehicle had been parked and there were no independent eye-witness of the recovery of the vehicle or of Attaullah procuring the key of the vehicle from a hidden place inside the roadside hotel. There was no evidence adduced to establish the motive. There was no evidence brought on record that Attaullah had stolen other vehicles. Neither Irfan Ullah (whose affidavit was presented as Ex-PJ stating that he had handed over a SIM registered in his name to Attaullah) was investigated as an accused person or presented before the court Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 8 as a witness, nor Zubair (who allegedly aided and abetted Attaullah in selling stolen cars and was visited by Attaullah on 22.02.2018 after Junaid Mustafa had been murdered) was investigated as an accused or produced as a witness. The prosecution recovered no CCTV footage from cameras installed in Street 79, G-13/1, even though Noman Wahab, the night watchman, had testified that the house at the corner of the street had CCTV cameras installed. The prosecution also collected no evidence from the Safe City Cameras installed in Islamabad to determine the movement and route of Junaid Mustafa’s car. Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the prosecution’s case was based on suspicion alone and the extra-judicial testimony attributed to Attaullah was procured while he was in detention and was not voluntarily given. He submitted that benefit of doubt ought to be given to the appellant and given the lack of evidence implicating the appellant in murder or robbery the appellant was liable to be acquitted.

10. The learned State Counsel submitted that while the case was one of the circumstantial evidence, the complete chain linking Attaullah to the murder of Junaid Mustafa had been established through reliable evidence. He made the following submissions. Attaullah’s CNIC was found at the place of occurrence. The Investigating Officer got the profile photo of Attaullah from the Careem database on the basis of the number linked to the profile that ordered the Careem cab. The night watchman Noman Wahab recalled that Attaullah had previously been involved in property business for which he used to visit G-13. This established that Attaullah was familiar with the location where he asked the Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 9 deceased Junaid Mustafa to drop him off. The cell phone which had the SIM through which the Careem Cab had been ordered was found in possession of Attaullah when he was arrested on 24.02.2018 driving another stolen vehicle. This established that Attaullah was in the business of stealing vehicles and he was in possession of the device through which the Careem Cab being driven by Junaid Mustafa had been ordered. While a forensic examination of the cell phone had not been undertaken, the learned Sessions Judge had himself taken judicial notice of the fact that the phone in question was in the use of Attaullah by switching on the phone during the trial and determining that the App through which the Careem Cab had been ordered was installed on the cell phone, which cell phone had also photos of Attaullah. Attaullah while in police custody led to the recovery of the vehicle, the key for which he had hidden inside the roadside hotel and the location of the key was in his exclusive knowledge. The recovery of the vehicle thus established that Attaullah had robbed the vehicle. The murder weapon was then recovered from the vehicle which was last used by Attaullah and locked by him and such recovery linked Attaullah to the murder of the deceased Junaid Mustafa and the robbery of the vehicle.

11. Let us consider the fault lines in the sequence of events and the evidence as produced by the prosecution. The incident took place at 03.00 am on 22.02.2018 at the corner of Street 79, G-13/1 and service road of G-13/1. Muhammad Hanif ASI (PW-9) was the first person who reached the place of occurrence, after which the body of the deceased was removed through Rescue 1122. Muhammad Hanif (PW-9) remained at the place of Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 10 occurrence and witnessed the recoveries of empties as well as the CNIC of Attaullah at around 11.30 am when Muhammad Riaz Gondal, Inspector/I.O (PW-13) reached there along with the deceased’s brother/complainant, Sohail Mustafa (PW-7). The site map suggests that recoveries were made from the edge of the service road even though the place of occurrence was not cordoned off. And the recoveries were not made by Muhammad Hanif ASI (PW-9), who first arrived at the place of occurrence at 03.20 am, but the empties and the CNIC of Attaullah just sat on a functional public road to be recovered by Muhammad Riaz Gondal, Inspector (PW-13) at around 11.30 am.

12. It is perplexing that according to the prosecution’s case, Attaullah, after murdering Junaid Mustafa, drove the vehicle out of Islamabad Capital Territory all the way to Mardan, KP, to consult with Zubair (his accomplice in selling stolen vehicles), but he did not hide the stolen vehicle with Zubair or in any other place in KP, but drove back in the same vehicle to park it not very far from the murder site. While doing so he stopped at the bridge over Attock River and threw deceased’s cell phone and wallet into the river so that it could not be recovered. But he retained the cell phone linked with SIM No. 0335-5167487 through which he had ordered the Cab in his own possession enabling the police authorities to link him to the murder. He drove the robbed vehicle back to Islamabad on the day of the murder knowing full well that he had snatched it from somebody he had murdered and found it convenient to park the vehicle adjacent to roadside hotel coowned and co-managed by his own father. And further he found it convenient to deposit the key in a drawer within such hotel. He Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 11 was then arrested by virtue of information provided by an informer driving another stolen vehicle. And at such time the cell phone he used to order the Careem Cab was in his personal possession along with another cell phone. This sequence of events does not appeal to a prudent mind. If the motive was to rob Junaid Mustafa of his vehicle, which was to be sold on the blackmarket, and Junaid Mustafa got shot because he resisted the robbery, why would the appellant drive the vehicle all the way to Mardan from where it was to be disposed of with the help of Zubair and then drive it all the way back and park it next to his father’s roadside hotel? It also makes no sense that while Attaullah had the presence of mind to dispose of cell phones and wallet of the deceased in the Attock River he would retain the cell phone he used to order the Careem Cab to facilitate the establishment of a link between the murder of Junaid Mustafa and himself.

13. It is equally incomprehensible why the accused would leave the murder weapon under the driver seat in the robbed vehicle. While Munir Khan, ASI (PW-5) testified that he witnessed Attaullah recovering the car key from inside the roadside hotel, as was testified by Muhammad Riaz Gondal (PW-13). However, the police party chose not to affiliate any private witnesses with the recovery. Given that the key was not being recovered from an isolated place but from inside a functional roadside hotel during day time, it is inconceivable that there was nobody present at the hotel at the time of such recovery.

14. More inscrutable than the circumstantial evidence produced by the prosecution are the acts of omission by the Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 12 Investigators. Noman Wahab (PW-8), the night watchman, testified that there were CCTV cameras installed at the corner house of the Street 79, G-13/1. But the footage from such cameras was not procured to see if it provided any leads. The vehicle was driven outside of Islamabad all the way to Mardan, KP, and back to Islamabad but no footage was procured from Safe City Cameras installed across Islamabad to determine the time at which the vehicle left Islamabad Capital Territory and when it returned and who was the person driving it.

15. The cell phone through which the Careem Cab driven by Junaid Mustafa had been ordered was registered in the name of Irfan Ullah, who was neither included in the investigation as an accused, nor was produced as a witness, even though his affidavit was retained and adduced by Muhammad Riaz Gondal (PW-13) wherein he had purportedly stated that he had handed over the SIM to Attaullah and that his sister was going to be married to Attaullah. If such affidavit were to be believed, Irfan Ullah was a key witness to support the prosecution’s case and help establish the presence of the appellant as a last customer driven by the deceased Junaid Mustafa and possibly help to support the prosecution’s story that Attaullah’s motive was to generate funds for his impending wedding with Irfan Ullah’s sister. There was nothing on record to establish that the prosecution made any efforts to adopt coercive measures to procure the presence of Irfan Ullah before the court.

16. The prosecution also did not investigate Zubair. Even if Zubair had no part to play in the murder, he would have been a Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 13 key witness to establish the prosecution story that Attaullah visited him on 22.02.2018 after the murder along with the stolen vehicle and had also shared his plans of selling stolen vehicles to generate funds of his wedding. No other witness was produced to establish that Attaullah was in the business of stealing vehicles and selling them. If the purpose of the robbery was to sell the vehicle stolen from Junaid Mustafa at gunpoint, it would make no sense for Attaullah to bring the vehicle back into Islamabad instead of disposing it of in KP once he had successfully driven it there. Was Attaullah not aware that the vehicle was linked to the virtual system managed by Careem and the police authorities would be looking for such vehicle, which is why he disposed of the deceased’s cell phone in Attock river? The cell phone recovered from Attaullah was not subjected to any forensic examination. A forensic examination of the Careem App installed in such phone together with the examination of the system maintained at the offices of Careem would have established that the App in question was used in ordering the vehicle being driven by the deceased. A forensic examination of the cell phone which was not registered in Attaullah’s name could have established that the phone was in fact in the personal use of Attaullah and the photos in the phone were such that could only have been taken by some body using the phone. For such purpose the prosecution could have produced expert testimony before the learned trial court. However such lacunae were apparently filled by the learned Sessions Judge taking judicial notice of the use of the cell phone by switching it on and satisfying himself while conducting the trial that the Careem App was installed on the phone and the photos in the Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 14 phone were such that it appeared that the phone had been in Attaullah’s personal use.

17. The CDR date produced by the prosecution does not present a consistent picture. Once it had been established through reliable evidence that the phone in question used to order the Careem Cab was in possession and use of Attaullah the CDR could then establish his whereabouts before and after the murder and robbery. It was the prosecution’s case that two cell phones (having SIMs No. 0335-5167487 and 0349-0999345 as reflected in Ex-PC) were recovered from Attaullah’s personal possession at the time of his arrest. If these two phones were in his possession at the relevant time, their location according to the CDR data should have been identical. Likewise the location reflected in the CDR for the cell phone in use of the deceased ought to have matched the location on Attaullah’s phone up until such point when the deceased’s phone was dumped in the Attock river. Thus, expert testimony could have been presented analyzing the CDR data to establish that the location of the cell phone in the possession of Attaullah and that which belonged to the deceased and remained in the stolen vehicle had identical location, and further the CDR analysis checked out the prosecution’s story re whereabouts of Attualullah after the murder up until his arrest on 24.02.2018. None of the above was however done.

18. The prosecution produced four independent witnesses. Qaiser Qayyum (PW-3), as the Security Manager of Careem Company, who exhibited Careem Company’s record and could only testify to what anyone could learn from the data maintained Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 15 by the Careem Company as reflected on a printed document. Sohail Mustafa (PW-7), the complainant and brother of the deceased Junaid Mustafa, was a Head Constable in Punjab Police and not a witness to the occurrence and had received a call in the early hours of 22.02.2018 regarding the sad news of his brother’s murder. Noman Wahab (PW-8) was the night watchman in whose presence the deceased breathed his last. His testimony was limited to hearing three fire shots and not witnessing who shot the deceased. He testified that he could not recognize in view of photo on the CNIC but did recognize Attaullah based on the profile photo procured by Inspector Muhammad Riaz Gondal (PW-13) from the Careem system and then recalled that Attaullah had been discharging property services in the locality. While he was at the place of occurrence at the time of the murder, he was not made to witness the recovery of Attaullah’s CNIC from the place of occurrence. And Farman Jalil (PW-12) testified that Attaullah visited the shop in which the said witness was employed to have his pistol cleaned, but as Attaullah did not possess a licensed weapon, Farma Jalil declined to provide the relevant service. His testimony included no details with regard to the nature of the pistol or otherwise linked Attaullah to the murder weapon. Farman Jalil testified that Muhammad Riaz Gondal (PW-13) visited his shop on 26.02.2022. It emerges from the record that such visit was prompted by information provided by Attaullah while in police custody and such visit predated the recovery of the murder weapon by one day. All it suggests is that Attaullah might have had one unlicensed weapon.

Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 16 19. “Evidence in criminal proceedings is the means whereby the truth of a matter may be established…direct evidence is that which … proves the existence of the fact in issue without inference or presumption” (Corpus Juris Secundum Criminal Law, Vol 22-A, Para 655). Circumstantial evidence on the other hand is the evidence which tends to prove a disputed fact on the basis of other connected facts, that lead to the inference that the fact that is to be proved reasonably follows and can be inferred on the basis of facts which have been proved.

20. Let us consider the law laid down by the august Supreme Court in relation to circumstantial evidence and benefit of doubt. It is settled law that last seen evidence is a weak form of circumstantial evidence (see for example Fazal Elahi alias Sajawal Vs. The Crown (PLD 1953 FC 214), Rehmat alias Rahman alias Waryam alias Badshah Vs. The State (PLD 1977 SC 515) and Naqibullah Vs. The State (PLD 1978 SC 21)).

21. It has been held by the august Supreme Court that punishments can be awarded on the basis of circumstantial evidence (See for example Jafar Ali Vs. State (1998 SCMR 2669) and Israr Ali Vs. State (2007 SCMR 525)). It was however emphasized by the august Supreme Court, while relying on Lejzor Vs. The Queen (PLD 1952 PC 119) and Fazal Elahi Vs. Crown (PLD 1953 PC 214), in Hashim Qasim Vs. State (2017 SCMR 986) that “circumstantial evidence may sometimes appear to be conclusive but it must always be narrowly examined, Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 17 if only because this count of evidence may be fabricated in order to cast suspicion on another …”.

22. It was held in Sh. Muhammad Amjad Vs. The State (PLD 2003 SC 704) that “death sentence can be awarded on circumstantial evidence, provided all circumstances constituted a chain and no link is missing and their combined effect is that the guilt of the accused is established beyond any shadow of doubt.” It was emphasized that last seen evidence was a weak form of circumstantial evidence which “must be accepted with great caution and is to be scrutinized minutely for reaching a conclusion that no plausible conclusion could be drawn therefrom accepting guilt of the accused”. In this case the court had approving the cited dicta from Charan Singh Vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh (AIR 1967 SC 520) wherein it had been held by the Indian Supreme Court that in a case of circumstantial evidence “circumstances should be of such a nature as to reasonably exclude every hypothesis but the one proposed to be proved i.e. chain of evidence must be complete…”. It was held in Muhammad Hussain Vs. State (2011 SCMR 1127) that “it is required that each piece of circumstantial evidence shall be supported by independent corroboration, which shall, by itself, be sufficient to establish guilt. However, each circumstance shall be so connected with each other that it shall make one complete chain, without there being any broken link.”

23. In order to punish the accused in the instant case the prosecution needed to establish circumstantial evidence in a manner that no prudent mind could entertain any reasonable Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 18 doubt regarding the culpability of the accused. This the prosecution has not done. As has been discussed in the reappraisal of the evidence undertaken by this Court above the prosecution’s case is almost entirely based on an investigation driven by the extrajudicial confessions made by the appellant, Attaullah, while in police custody, which confessions are also conflicting.

24. It was held by the august Supreme Court while interpreting section 103 of Cr.P.C in Mir Muhammad Vs. State (1995 SCMR 614) that “police officers are as good witnesses as any other citizens …” and that in a recovery affected on the pointation of the accused there was no need to associate two respectable inhabitants of the locality for purposes of Article 40 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984. The same principle was reiterated by the august Supreme Court in Muhammad Akbar Vs. State (1995 SCMR 693), State Vs. Shankar (1997 SCMR 1000) and Asif Mahmood Vs. The State (2005 SCMR 515).

25. It is on the basis of the law in relation to Section 103 of Cr.P.C that the prosecution had argued that it need not have associated any private witnesses while affecting the recovery of the vehicle or its key. Notwithstanding the general principle laid down by the august Supreme Court, it still makes no sense that where recovery is being affected from a public place (i.e. a functional roadside hotel) and it is being affected at a time when such hotel ought to have been inhabited by owners, servers and workers, the police would not associate anyone while affecting the recovery. Or the police would not interrogate and collect evidence Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 19 from the owners and managers of such hotel to determine when the robbed vehicle wanted in a murder investigation was parked there and how come the key of the vehicle parked close to the hotel ended up being placed inside such hotel, and all this went unnoticed for at least five days till 27.02.2018 when the recovery was affected on Attaullah’s pointation.

26. In the instant case there is no independent evidence with regard to recoveries. The recovery of the cell phone allegedly creating a link between Attaullah and the deceased used to order the Careem Cab was recovered from Attaullah at the time of his arrest on 24.02.2018 and was witnessed exclusively by the police arresting party. The CNIC and the empties recovered from the place of occurrence were recovered eight hours after the occurrence from a public place. And the robbed vehicle, which was recovered from public place and had the murder weapon, was also witnessed exclusively by the police party investigating the case. The murder weapon was recovered under the driver seat of the stolen vehicle on 27.02.2018 and it was after the arrest of Attaullah on 24.02.2018 and the recovery of the murder weapon on 27.02.2018 that the empties recovered from the place of occurrence on 22.02.2018 were sent for forensic examination on 27.02.2018 (which is also why the learned Sessions Court found the recovery of the murder weapon and empties inconsequential).

27. The august Supreme Court in State Vs. Mushtaq Ahmad (PLD 1973 SC 418) had dwelled on the concept of grant of benefit of doubt and it held that, “law allows to persons accused of criminal offences the benefit of “reasonable" and not of Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 20 imaginary doubts. What is reasonable doubt is not a question of law: it is essentially a question for human judgment by a prudent person to be found in each case, in the light of day to day experience in life, after, taking in account fully all the facts and circumstances appearing on the entire record.” In Nazim Khan Vs. The State (1984 SCMR 1092) it was emphasized that benefit of doubt arising from discrepancies and inconsistencies must be given to the accused for safe administration of criminal justice and it was held in the case that, “there is conspicuous lack of independent corroboration in accordance with the principles governing safe administration of criminal justice the appellants are entitled to benefit of doubt”. Conviction of the accused in the case was set-aside. In Muhammad Akram Vs. State (2009 SCMR 230) it was held that “if there is circumstance which created reasonable doubt in a prudent mind about the guilt of the accused, then the accused would be entitled to the benefit of doubt not as a matter of grace and concession but as a matter of right.”

28. Within the context of grant of benefit of doubt it was held by the august Supreme in Muhammad Shah Vs. The State (2010 SCMR 1009) that where two interpretations of the evidence adduced before a court are possible, one favoring the accused and the other favoring the prosecution, then the interpretation more favorable to the accused is required to be taken into account. It was further emphasized that all incriminating pieces of evidence available on record in the examination-in-chief, cross-examination or re-examination of witnesses are required to be put to the accused and that, “if any Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 21 piece of evidence is not put to the accused in his statement under section 342 Cr.P.C, and the same cannot be used against him for his conviction.” The same principle that any piece of evidence not put to the accused in his statement under section 342 of Cr.P.C cannot be used against him was reiterated in Muhammad Shah Vs. State (PLJ 2011 SC 348). With regard to confessions made before police authorities it was held in Imran alias Dully Vs. The State (2015 SCMR 155) that, “extrajudicial confession has never been considered sufficient for recording conviction on a capital charge unless it is strongly corroborated by tangible evidence coming from unimpeachable source...”

29. Let us apply these principles to the facts of the present case. There is no unbroken chain of circumstantial evidence produced by the prosecution on the basis of which Attaullah can be found culpable for having murdered the deceased or indulging in armed robbery. The recoveries on the basis of which circumstantial case is built against Attaullah have no independent corroboration and have been witnessed exclusively by police witnesses. There is no eye-witness of Attaullah getting into the Careem Cab driven by the deceased or getting off the vehicle in G-13/1. No one witnessed Attaullah shooting the deceased and no one witnessed Attaullah driving the robbed vehicle while it was driven all the way to KP and back to ICT to be parked close to a roadside hotel in G-16/4. There is no direct evidence of Attaullah possessing or using the cell phone used to order the Careem Cab driven by the deceased. Neither Careem App installed on the cell phone with SIM No. 0335-5167487 was examined, nor the cell phone itself establish that it was in the possession and use of Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 22 Attaullah. This void has been filled by judicial notice of the relevant facts being verified by the learned Sessions Court itself. It is a settled principle that the power to take judicial notice of a fact as proof of such fact is to be exercised with extreme caution as at stake is the right of the accused who would have no opportunity to rebut the notice taken by the court itself. In the present case a foundational fact that the cell phone used to order the Careem Cab driven by the deceased was in the use of Attaullah and the Careem App used to order the vehicle was installed on such phone has been determined conclusively by the learned Session Court itself by virtue of taking judicial notice of it. This also militates against the right of fair trial of an accused guaranteed under Article 10A of the Constitution as well as the law laid down in relation to putting all incriminating evidence to an accused under section 342 of Cr.P.C. A Presiding trial court Judge is no forensic or IT expert and has no basis, in the absence of expert testimony to analyze the footprints of an App and data installed in a phone, to determine the identity of a user of the phone. The accused also had no occasion to rebut any inference drawn by the court itself. Taking judicial notice of a critical link within the chain of circumstantial evidence amounts to filling in a lacuna and militates against safe administration of justice.

30. What emerges from the above is that it is entirely possible that Attaullah booked the cab and it ended up killing the deceased while attempting to steal the vehicle at gunpoint. But unless Attaullah’s extrajudicial confessions before the police and the investigation undertaken by the police on the basis of such disclosure can be deemed reliable it is equally possible that all the Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 23 evidence used to build a circumstantial case against Attaullah was planted by investigators in a high-profile murder case in which the police authorities were under significant media scrutiny and public pressure to quickly identify the culprit. And Attaullah became a scapegoat who as per the defenses’s suggestion in the crossexamination of Muhammad Riaz Gondal (PW-13) had been under arrest on 22.02.2018 as opposed to 24.02.0218. Where there are two interpretations possible of the evidence, the court cannot pick the one that disfavors the accused, as in case of such doubt the benefit of the same must be given to the accused as a matter of right. As this opinion reflects, this Court is concerned with both, the sufficiency of evidence and the trustworthiness of evidence produced and therefore finds that the prosecution has failed to prove through the circumstantial evidence adduced that the appellant, Attaullah, was guilty of the offence of murder and armed robbery. This Court also finds that the learned Sessions Court taking judicial notice to prove that Attaullah was using the cell phone through which the Careem Cab driven by the deceased was booked caused prejudice to the appellant, undermined his right to fair trial and compromised safe administration of justice. We therefore find that the judgment is liable to be set-aside due to lack of proof of guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The appellant, Attaullah, is entitled to be acquitted.

31. The purpose of administration of criminal justice is not to convict the accused but to convict the guilty. We are cognizant of the fact that a 26-year-old lost his life while trying to make ends meet and the release of an individual convicted for the murder of a citizen can erode public confidence in the criminal justice Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 24 system. However when it comes to retaining public confidence in the justice system on the one hand and the right of a citizen to be presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond reasonable doubt through a fair trial, a court must err on the right of side of the individual’s right to life and liberty. Judicial decisions cannot be informed by the desire to gain public approval by enhancing the conviction rate in relation to gruesome crime even where the evidence as produced before the Court does not support returning a guild verdict.

32. This Court, however, feels that in view of the nature of the offence and the use of the electronic devices therein, the failure of the prosecution in building a case beyond reasonable doubt is either due to the complicity of the Investigating Officers or their utter incompetence. It is beyond comprehension why the cell phone purportedly used to order the Careem Cab was not subjected to forensic examination to establish conclusively that the Careem App through which the Cab driven by the deceased was ordered was installed on the cell phone attributed to Attaullah. And why forensic investigation of such cell phone was not undertaken to generate expert testimony to the effect that the device was in use of Attaullah as alleged by the prosecution. It is equally inexplicable as to why the Investigating Officers would not procure CCTV footage from the cameras installed in the street at the edge of which the murder was committed or why footage from Safe City Cameras was not procured to determine and corroborate the facts of the case and the identity of the individual driving the vehicle after the murder of the deceased. It is also incomprehensible why no finger printing was done to lift prints Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 25 from the vehicle driven by the accused from the place of occurrence all the way to Mardan, KP and back to G-16/4, Islamabad. In the event that fingerprints of the appellant were found in the car, especially on the driving wheel, would establish his presence within such vehicle as a driver and would be a key piece of evidence. It is also unfathomable as to why Irfan Ullah, in whose name the SIM of the relevant cell phone was registered, was not made part of the investigation or his presence not ensured as a witness before the learned trial court. And also why Zubair, who is alleged to be an aider and abettor of Attaullah in selling stolen vehicles and who Attaullahh met on 22.02.2018 after the murder of the deceased along with the stolen car in Mardan on 22.02.2018 was not made part of the investigation and not produced before the learned trial court. If the prosecution story is assumed to be true, there is no reason why circumstantial evidence could not be gathered and proved such that the chain connecting the accused with the murder of the deceased could be established beyond a shadow of doubt and in each link in the chain could be supported by credible corroborating evidence. This Court therefore finds that the Investigating Team in the case is liable to be proceeded against by the Inspector General of Police Islamabad Capital Territory, and ought not be given any investigation responsibility, if they are retained in active service pending disciplinary proceedings. The Court further finds that the manner in which investigations are being conducted in ICT are undermining public faith in the ability of our criminal justice system to hold criminals to account.

Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 26 33. This Court is also cognizant of its powers under section 375 of Cr.P.C read with section 428, to order further inquiry or take additional evidence, where in question is the guilt or innocence of a person, to discharge its responsibility under section 561-A of Cr.P.C to secure the ends of justice. However forensic examination of the relevant cell phone at this stage alone would prove nothing as the remaining links in the circumstantial case built by the prosecution are equally vulnerable and lacking credibility. The vehicle in question was released on superdari on 10.03.2018 to the father of the deceased and is not useful for purposes of further inquiry and fingerprints analysis etc. Irfan Ullah the owner of the SIM used in the cell phone and Attaullah’s cousin and Zubair, Attaullah’s alleged accomplice in disposing of stolen vehicles, were never charged. In these facts and circumstances the hands of the courts despite its powers under section 375 read together with sections 428 and 561-A of Cr.P.C. cannot be of much use. The investigation had so badly bungled that nothing short of an investigation from scratch would do.

34. In view of the above, we allow Criminal Appeal No. 171/2019 filed by Attaullah, and answer the Murder Reference in the negative and set-aside the impugned judgment dated 18.05.2019. The appellant, Attaullah, stands acquitted from the charge framed against him by the learned Sessions Court by orders dated 25.06.2018 and 12.10.2018 and shall be released forthwith if not required in any other case.

35. The Court can however not act as an efficient bystander while releasing the accused on the basis of benefit of doubt due to Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 27 the failure of the prosecution to conduct the investigation competently. The Court does owe a duty to the society that has an interest in ensuring that those involved in crime do not go unpunished and justice is served not only to deter the criminals but also to bring solace to the legal heirs of citizens who are victims of brutal crime.

36. Protecting the role of investigators and prosecutors falls primarily within the domain of the Executive. But where the Executive does not seem to be discharging such responsibility and the effect is that the right of citizens to life, liberty, dignity and dispensation of justice is undermined, it is the Judiciary’s responsibility as the enforcement machinery re fundamental rights and provisions of the Constitution, to direct that remedial action be taken. To discharge our duty as the dispensers of justice in accordance with law, we feel that following instructions must be issued:

(1) The Police Order, 2002, is in force in Islamabad Capital Territory as has been observed by this Court in Mahera Sajid Vs. Station House Officer, Police Station Shalimar and others (2018 CLC 1858) and a key feature of the Police Order is that duties of watch and ward must be separated from the duties of investigation. Police Order, 2002, envisages functional specialization. The Ministry of Interior and the Inspector General of Police, ICT must therefore ensure that the ICT Police is structured such that the duties of watch and ward Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 28 and the duties of investigation are separated within a period of no longer than six months.

(2) The accused in criminal matters are frequently released as courts extend benefit of doubt to them as required by law, which doubt is more often than not generated due to faulty investigations. The Ministry of Interior and the Inspector General of Police, ICT will ensure that all officers of Islamabad Police deputed for purposes of conducting investigation have received basic investigative training, including inter alia, training on how to ensure crime scene preservation, prior to them being posted to an office that entails an investigation role. Such training mechanism shall be put in place within a period of six months.

(3) Doubt is created in the prosecution’s case due to lack of proper preservation of recoveries and lack of analysis in relation to incriminating material. The ICT Police shall put together a Standard Operating Manual to ensure that all recoveries which are to be used in building a case against an accused are not left within the custody of the investigators or the custody of the relevant Police Station. The Ministry of Interior and ICT Police shall put in place a creditable and verifiable mechanism for storing recoveries in criminal matters during investigation, trial and appellate proceedings, such that sanctity of the Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 29 recovered item is beyond doubt and the system of checks and balances inspires confidence and recoveries cannot be doctored or planted. The control of the depository for the recoveries shall neither be with the police station nor with the investigation team. Such system shall be put in place with in a period of one year.

(4) The Standard Operating Manual will also include guidelines in the manner in which the evidence is to be generated from the recovered items, including the timing of sending empties as well as weapons for forensic investigation in a manner that such recoveries do not become inconsequential. The Manual will include mandatory instructions re lifting fingerprints from recoveries affected and/or place of occurrence and undertaking forensic examination of electronic devices and generating required expert evidence especially where electronic devices become relevant.

(5) The Ministry of Interior and the Inspector General of Police, ICT will ensure that the investigators are also equipped with body cameras especially in cases where recoveries are made on the basis of disclosures made by the accused when in police custody and to ensure that there is proper video evidence of such recovery to satisfy the conscience of the court that recoveries are not attributed to the Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 30 accused through use of coercive means and torture and are independently verifiable through corroborating evidence. The guidelines in this regard must be mandatory and disregarding them must entail penal consequences for the officers disregarding them.

(6) Frequently doubt is cast due to lack of independent corroborating evidence and the only material available in support of the prosecution case is the account within police diaries. It is settled law that such material does not constitute evidence in cases of circumstantial evidence and thus the court has nothing to rely on but suspicion based on prosecution’s account. The Ministry of Interior and the Inspector General of Police, ICT will initiate the process of digitization of police dairies such that each entry within such diaries has an electronic timestamp which cannot be manipulated subsequently. This will give greater credibility to the real time account recorded by the Investigating Officers while undertaking investigations especially in cases of circumstantial evidence. Such process, which has already been undertaken to some extent by the Punjab Government through work of Punjab Information Technology Board (PTIB), shall be undertaken within the ICT within a period of one year.

Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 31 (7) The Ministry of Law and Office of the Chief Commissioner ICT shall ensure that an appropriate number of prosecutors are appointed and trained for prosecution of criminal matters within the ICT, and the Chief Commissioner together with Ministry of Interior and Inspector General of Police ICT will ensure that a qualified prosecutor is staffed with an investigation team in each case at the investigation stage to ensure that evidence collected during the investigation is admissible and sufficient for successful prosecution of the charge. And further to determine what charge ought to be included within the charge sheet filed before the court in view of the evidence collected so that those accused of criminal charges can be successfully prosecuted and convicted. An appropriate system for training and staffing of the prosecutors as stated above shall be put in place within a period of one year.

37. Let a copy of this judgment be sent to the Secretary Ministry of Interior, Secretary Ministry of Law and Justice, Chief Commissioner ICT and Inspector General of Police ICT for compliance. Each one of them will file progress reports every three months for perusal in Chambers and a final compliance report within the time period prescribed for compliance in Para 36.

38. The Inspector General of Police ICT will file a report of the inquiry and any subsequent disciplinary action if any, in Crl. Appeal No. 171/2019 & M.R No. 13/2019 P a g e | 32 relation to the conduct of the Investigating Officers in the instant case within a period of three months for perusal in Chambers. 10. The above mentioned facts spell out that no explanation was available with the appellant, therefore, he simply answered the same “it is incorrect”, in such scenario, it is the primary duty of the trial court to check the veracity of every statement, article or evidence to explore the possibility to reach at just decision, which trial court did in this case, especially when the mobile phone was recovered from accused at the time of his arrest, was switched on, which provide details of his personal photographs and videos like selfies and videos, which were examined by the trial court and also referred above in para-08 of this judgment.

11. This entire exercise is not barred by any law, though it seems to be the failure on the part of I.O, who did not get mobile phone forensically examined from an expert of National Forensic Science Agency, but such failure does not impose any restriction upon the trial Court to consider the recovered phone of the accused on common prudence of the trial Court. The wisdom has to be considered in terms of Section 540 Cr.P.C. where Court had powers to summon material witness or examine any evidence at any stage of any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under Cr.P.C. or summons any person as a witness, or examine any person in attendance, though not summoned as a witness, or recall and re-examine any person already examined if his evidence appears to it essential to the just decision of the case. Such aspect gives wide discretionary powers, which could only be exercised in a mandatory manner to ascertain the truth in order to reach at Crl. Appeal No.171-2019 and Murder Reference No.13-2019 Page | 9 fair conclusion of the case. No doubt the trial Court has unfettered powers to examine any person as a witness at any stage of any inquiry, trial or other proceedings obligatory for Court to do so when it was essential for just decision of case and under this analogy, the powers are clearly been explained in Criminal Procedure Code, where trial Court can look into the incriminating articles recovered from the accused like mobile phone P-6 in this case. This Court has taken guidance in this regard from the case law reported as PLD 1984 SC 95 (Muhammad Azam vs. Muhammad Iqbal), 1987 SCMR 886 (Painda Gul vs. The State).

18. Circumstantial evidence may sometimes be conclusive but it must always be narrowly examined. It is of the utmost importance that the circumstances should be ascertained with minute care and caution, before any conclusion or interference adverse to the accused person is drawn. The process of inference and deduction involved in such cases is of a delicate and perplexing character, liable to numerous causes of fallacy. This danger points the need for the great caution in accepting proof of the facts and circumstances before they are held to be established for the purposes for drawing inferences therefrom. A mere concurrence of circumstances some or all of which are supported by defective or inadequate evidence can create a specious appearance, leading to fallacious inferences. Hence, it is necessary that only such circumstances should be accepted as the basis of inferences that are, on careful examination of the evidence found to be well established. A high quality of evidence is, therefore, required to prove the facts and circumstance from which the guilt of the accused person is to be drawn. Reliance is placed on the cases titled “Lejzor Teper v. Queen” [PLD 1952 SC 117], “Fazal Ellahi v. Crown” [PLD 1953 FC 214], “Saeed Ahmed Hamdani v. Muhammad Irfan and others [PLD 1986 SC 690].

19. There are chances of fabricating evidence in cases that are based solely on circumstantial evidence before the Court in such cases should take extra care and caution to examine the evidence with pure Page-13 judicial approach on strict legal standards to satisfy itself about its proof, probative value and reliability. Where there are apparent indications of possibility of fabricating evidence by the Investigating Officer in making the case, the court must be watchful against the trap which may mislead to draw a false inference and satisfy itself about the fear and genuine collection of such evidence. The failure of the Court to observe such care and caution can adversely affect the proper and safe administration of criminal justice. Reliance is placed on “Hashim Qasim v. The State” [2017 SCMR 986], “Fayyaz Ahmed v. The State” [2017 SCMR 2026].

20. The settled approach to deal with the question as to sufficiency of circumstantial evidence for conviction of the accused person is this; if, on the facts and circumstance proved no hypothesis consistent with the innocence of the accused person can be suggested, the case is fit for conviction of the accused person on such conclusion; however, if such facts and circumstances can be reconciled with any reasonable hypothesis compatible with the innocence of the accused, the case is to be treated one of insufficient evidence resulting in acquittal of accused person. Reliance is placed on the cases titled “Siraj v. Crown” [PLD 1956 FC 123], “Muhammad Nazir Hossain v. The State” [1969 SCMR 388].

21. Circumstantial evidence in a murder case should be like a well-knit chain, one end of which touches the dead body of the deceased and the other the neck of the accused. No link in chain of circumstances should be broken and the circumstances should be such as cannot be explained away on any reasonable hypothesis other than guilt of accused person. Chain of such facts and circumstances has to be completed to establish guilt of accused person beyond reasonable doubt and to make the plea of being innocent incompatible with the weight of evidence against him. Any link missing from the chain breaks the whole chain and renders the same unreliable; in that event Page-14 conviction cannot be safely recorded especially on a capital charge, therefore, if the circumstantial evidence is found not of the said standard and quality it will be highly unsafe to rely upon the same for conviction rather not to rely upon said evidence will be a better and safe course. Reliance is placed on the cases titled “Saeed v. Muhammad Irfan” [PLD 1986 SC 690], “Imran v. The State” [2015 SCMR 155], “Azeem Khan v. Mujahid Khan” [2016 SCMR 274].

22. It is held by the Supreme Court in the case titled “Maqsood Alam and another v. The State and others” [2024 SCMR 156] that it is settled principle of law that the conviction must be based on unimpeachable, trustworthy and reliable evidence. Any doubt arising in prosecution case is to be resolved in favour of the accused and burden of proof is always on prosecution to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt. It is also an established principle of law and equity that it is better that 100 guilty persons should let off but one innocent person should not suffer. The peculiar facts and circumstances of the present case are sufficient to cast a shadow of doubt on the prosecution case, which entitles the petitioner benefit of the doubt not as a matter of grace and concession but as of right. For the accused to be afforded this right of the benefit of the doubt, it is not necessary that there should be many circumstances creating uncertainty and if there is only one doubt, the benefit of the same must go to the accused. Reliance is placed on Mst. Asia Bibi v. The State (PLD 2019 SC 64), Tariq Pervaiz v. The State (1995 SCMR 1345), Ayub Masih v. The State (PLD 2002 SC 1048) and Abdul Jabbar v. State (2019 SCMR 129).

23. The Supreme Court in the case titled “Naveed Asghar and two others v. The State” [PLD 2021 SC 600] has held that the frightful nature of crime should not blur the eyes of justice, allowing emotions triggered by the horrifying nature of the offence to prejudge the accused. Cases are to be decided on the basis of evidence and Page-15 evidence alone and not on the basis of sentiments and emotions. Gruesome, heinous or brutal nature of the offence may be relevant at the stage of awarding suitable punishment after conviction; but it is totally irrelevant at the stage of appraising or reappraising the evidence available on record to determine guilt of the accused person, as possibility of an innocent person having been wrongly involved in cases of such nature cannot be ruled out. An accused person is presumed to be innocent till the time he is proven guilty beyond reasonable doubt, and this presumption of his innocence continues until the prosecution succeeds in proving the charge against him beyond reasonable doubt on the basis of legally admissible, confidence inspiring, trustworthy and reliable evidence. No matter how heinous the crime, the constitutional guarantee of fair trial under Article 10A cannot be taken away from the accused. It is, therefore, duty of the court to assess the probative value (weight) of every piece of evidence available on record in accordance with the settled principles of appreciation of evidence, in a dispassionate, systematic and structured manner without being influenced by the nature of the allegations. Any tendency to strain or stretch or haphazardly appreciate evidence to reach a desired or popular decision in a case must be scrupulously avoided or else highly deleterious results seriously affecting proper administration of criminal justice will follow. It may be pertinent to underline here that the principles of fair trial have now been guaranteed as a Fundamental Right under Article 10-A of the Constitution and are to be read as an integral part of every subconstitutional legislative instrument that deals with determination of civil rights and obligations of, or criminal charge against, any person.

24. The evidence brought on record proves that the murder of an innocent person was committed. The occurrence is unseen. The who committed the murder? The prosecution was burdened with heavy duty to bring on record unimpeachable and undeniable circumstantial evidence to connect the appellant with the commission Page-16 offence beyond the shadow of doubt. The evidence brought on record by the prosecution in the instant case is deficient and inconsistent. Material evidence has either not been collected or given up, which has broken the chain raising serious doubts as to involvement of the appellant in the commission of offence. In the facts and circumstances of the case, the learned trial court has wrongly inflicted the conviction and sentence upon the appellant. The appellant ought to have been extended the benefit of doubt and should not have been punished for proving his innocence as it was duty of the prosecution to prove its case beyond the shadow of doubt. The prosecution has failed to bring home guilt of the appellant by producing cogent, reliable and trustworthy evidence in this regard.
25. I agree with the conclusion of acquittal arrived at by my learned brother Mr Justice Babar Sattar, J. and the directions contained in paragraph 36 of his opinion/judgment.

26. For what has been discussed above, the Criminal Appeal No.171/2019 titled “Attaullah v. The State & another” is allowed. Consequently the appellant (Attaullah) is acquitted of the charge. He be released forthwith if not required to be incarcerated in any other case. Murder Reference No.13/2019 titled “The State v. Attaullah” is, therefore, answered in the “negative”.
